title: C.S. Lewis Said Gender Is More Real Than Sex
author: Davis, J. Chase
summary: J. Chase Davis argues that C.S. Lewis's claim in Perelandra that gender is more real than sex is often misread as anticipating modern gender-identity theory, when it means nearly the opposite: masculinity and femininity are eternal realities in the mind of God that male and female bodies express, not constructs layered onto a neutral body. Drawing on guest Josh Herring's book Sons of Adam, Daughters of Eve, Davis traces how sex and gender swapped meanings across the twentieth century and connects that linguistic drift to the modern conviction, dated to 1789 and Simone de Beauvoir, that identity can be willed into being through technique. He credits this project with concrete costs, including fewer and later marriages and a reshaped single-income household, and frames Lewis's view as a needed corrective: gendered reality is received, not constructed.
points: Reinterprets Lewis's 'gender is more real than sex' as a claim about metaphysical reality prior to the body, not social construction.
Traces the etymological swap of 'sex' and 'gender' from the sixteenth century to the twentieth.
Links Simone de Beauvoir's 'woman is made, not born' thesis to concrete social costs: fewer marriages, delayed marriage, restructured single-income households.
Surfaces a genuine philosophical disagreement (Platonist vs. Aristotelian starting points) between the author and his guest.
quotes: He was not saying your body is an accident and your inner sense of self is the truth. He was saying the masculine and the feminine are real things that exist in the mind of God, and that male and female bodies are how those realities show up in the flesh.

In the sixteenth century, "sex" meant male and female. "Gender" meant kind, from the same root as generation. Then in the early twentieth century "sex" started to mean intercourse, and "gender" filled in the gap as a construction of identity.
Josh dates it to 1789 and the French Revolution: the conviction that through science and technique we can bend reality to fit what we want.

The cost has been fewer marriages, later marriages, more women than men in higher education and in Fortune 500 leadership, a doubling of unmarried men in a decade, and an economy restructured so that a single income no longer runs a household.
He asked me a diagnostic question: Plato or Aristotle? I said Aristotle. That is exactly where we split.
